analysis.one_liner: Shielded companies that shipped scrap for recycling from Superfund cleanup liability.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never left the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Superfund law, companies that 'arranged for' waste to go somewhere can be made to pay cleanup costs if that site later becomes contaminated — including companies that sold scrap for recycling. This bill would have exempted shippers of scrap paper, plastic, glass, textiles, rubber, scrap metal, and used batteries from that liability, as long as the material met a commercial grade, a market existed, and the shipper used reasonable care to check that the recycler was following environmental laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that generate and ship recyclable material — paper mills, beverage and food packagers, battery makers, and the scrap recycling trade — would stop facing cleanup bills when a recycling site they sold to turned out to be a toxic-waste problem. The bill's stated purposes included removing liability 'disincentives' to recycling and equalizing treatment of recycled versus virgin materials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Scrap shippers and the recycling trade

how_it_helps.text: Exempts anyone who arranged for recycling of scrap paper, plastic, glass, textiles, rubber, scrap metal, or spent batteries from Superfund cleanup liability under sections 107(a)(3) and 107(a)(4), if they prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the material met a commercial specification grade, a market existed, a substantial portion went toward a new saleable product, and it could replace virgin raw material.

Requires only 'reasonable care' about the receiving facility — weighing the price paid, the person's ability to detect problems, and inquiries to environmental agencies — and applies that care requirement only to transactions 90 days or more after enactment.

Adds a penalty: anyone who sues a protected shipper for contribution must pay that shipper's full defense costs, including attorney and expert witness fees, which would discourage others from trying to shift cleanup costs back to them.

analysis.who_pays: Cleanup costs at contaminated recycling sites would fall on the parties still liable — mainly the site owners and operators, the federal Superfund trust fund when no one else can pay, and neighboring communities left with partially funded cleanups. Weakening liability for generators also removes a financial incentive for them to check where their material ends up.

drawbacks.text: The exemption shifts cleanup costs away from the companies that generated and shipped the material onto site owners, the Superfund trust fund, and communities near contaminated sites, and reduces the 'polluter pays' financial incentive that made generators careful about the facilities they dealt with.

The bill itself acknowledges the downside of its carve-outs: the exemption disappears if the shipper had a reasonable basis to believe the material would be burned as fuel or the facility was out of compliance, if hazardous substances were added, or if material contained PCBs above 50 parts per million — a list of conditions showing how much contaminated material could otherwise flow under the shield.

Supporters' good-faith case: the existing liability rules were an 'unintended consequence' of the 1980 Superfund law that discouraged recycling, pushed scrap into landfills, and disadvantaged recycled material against virgin raw materials — a real cost to waste reduction goals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have made some transactions easier for recycling businesses and might modestly encouraged reuse, but its main effect was a targeted liability shield: companies that shipped scrap would stop paying for cleanups at contaminated recycling sites, and those costs would land on the Superfund trust fund, other liable parties, and communities near the sites. The bill contained exclusions and care standards that limited the worst abuses, but the core effect was moving cleanup costs from shippers of waste to the public and to smaller site owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, never got a single cosponsor, and the committee took no action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Warner introduced the bill on May 12, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No further action was taken — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no new liability shield for scrap shippers was created in this Congress; companies that send material to contaminated recycling sites remained potentially liable for cleanup costs, which benefits the Superfund trust fund and the public's interest in polluters paying for cleanups. Businesses in the recycling chain, however, did not get the liability relief they sought.

industries.industry: Scrap paper, plastic, glass, textile, and rubber shippers
industries.note: The bill would have exempted them from Superfund liability when recycling sites they sold to became contaminated, as long as material met a commercial grade and they used reasonable care. Their gain — escaping cleanup costs — is the public's cost at contaminated sites.

Spent batteries are named in the bill specifically; battery handlers would be shielded from cleanup liability if they followed federal battery regulations. Battery chemicals like lead and cadmium are persistent toxins, so cleanup costs they escaped would fall elsewhere.

Scrap metal transactions would be deemed recycling — and protected — if the metal wasn't melted first and future EPA standards were followed. This matters for old auto, radiator, and demolition scrap, a common pathway for lead and other hazardous substances at contaminated sites.

industries.industry: Owners and operators of contaminated sites
industries.note: The bill leaves owner and operator liability untouched, so site owners — including small property holders who unknowingly bought contaminated land — would continue to bear cleanup responsibility, and could not easily recover costs from protected shippers.
